column4: The section's moon follows the sun without taking its place; this ayah says neither sun can overtake moon nor night outstrip day, placing that following inside an inviolable celestial order.
The section defines غ ش و as covering and turns the night-day relay into pursuit; this ayah has God cover day with night as it pursues swiftly and subjects sun and moon.

The section distinguishes the sun as a radiating source from the moon that follows in measured stages; this ayah calls the sun radiance, the moon light, and assigns the moon phases for reckoning time.
The section's dawn splits night's blackness while night, sun, and moon keep measure; this ayah joins فَالِقُ ٱلْإِصْبَاحِ, night as repose, and sun and moon as calculation in one scene.
The section stages night as covering and day as making visible; this ayah effaces the sign of night and makes the sign of day مُبْصِرَةً so people can seek provision and count time.
The section's single face is alternately covered and disclosed in an ordered relay; this ayah wraps night over day and day over night while sun and moon each run to a fixed term.
This repeats the section's exact night action, وَٱلَّيْلِ إِذَا يَغْشَىٰ, making covering itself the object of the adjacent surah's oath.
The section's day uncovers the sun through the root ج ل و; this ayah swears by day when it تَجَلَّىٰ, the luminous counterpart to the preceding covering night.
The section says dawn-light is drawn out of night; this ayah directly pairs darkening the sky's night with bringing out its ضُحَىٰ.
The section hears the root of نَفْس in dawn's breathing; this ayah supplies the exact celestial image, وَٱلصُّبْحِ إِذَا تَنَفَّسَ.
The section finds in the family of س و ي the night when the moon becomes complete; this ayah swears by the moon إِذَا ٱتَّسَقَ, when it grows full.
The section hears succession in عُقْبَىٰ and in the moon following the sun; this ayah makes night and day خِلْفَةً, replacements for one another for remembrance and gratitude.
The section carries night's covering into the inward life as a veil over perception; this ayah places غِشَاوَةٌ over the unbelievers' eyes after heart and hearing are sealed.
The section explains دَسَّىٰهَا through hiding oneself and pushing another into earth; this ayah unites both acts as the father hides from his people and considers يَدُسُّهُۥ فِى ٱلتُّرَابِ.
The section contrasts a sign that opens eyes with the blindness Thamud chooses; this ayah calls the she-camel مُبْصِرَةً and says Thamud wronged her.
The section turns daylight and darkness into moral sight and blindness; this ayah says Thamud preferred blindness to guidance and was seized by a humiliating thunderbolt.
The section develops غَاشِيَة as punishment that covers a whole people; this ayah asks whether an enveloping punishment from God may come upon those who feel secure.
The section explains دمدمة as complete eradication of Thamud; this ayah states the corresponding result tersely: Thamud was left with nothing surviving.
The section links covering to collective destruction; in the same catalogue of destroyed peoples, this ayah describes the overturned city with the emphatic فَغَشَّىٰهَا مَا غَشَّىٰ.
The section makes daylight disclose and night cover one face; this ayah reverses the viewpoint, stripping day from night so that people suddenly stand in darkness.
The section presents the sun as a source moving through a measured order; this ayah gives the sun its appointed course and limit.
The section's following moon is understood through ordered stages; this ayah assigns the moon measured phases, preparing the non-overtaking rule in 36:40.
The section's night covers day through غ ش و; this ayah repeats that exact cosmic operation after describing the earth spread out beneath the sky.
The section begins with the spreading brightness of ضُحَىٰ; this ayah makes that same forenoon brightness an oath.
The section pairs spreading daylight with covering night; this ayah places night when it grows still beside the oath by forenoon in 93:1.
The section follows the moon within a coordinated sequence; this ayah opens another three-part celestial oath with the moon, continued by retreating night and revealing morning in 74:33-34.
The section's night belongs to a relay rather than a static darkness; this ayah swears by night as it turns away, between the moon of 74:32 and morning of 74:34.
The section describes dawn as night's covering being opened; this ayah completes the neighbouring sequence with morning when it shines clearly.
The section treats night and breathing dawn as successive movements; this ayah's night إِذَا عَسْعَسَ, whether advancing or receding, is the immediate counterpart to the dawn that breathes in 81:18.
The section tracks measured transitions of one light-bearing sky; this oath by twilight begins the sequence that moves through gathering night to the full moon in 84:17-18.
The section's night covers and gathers the visible world; this ayah swears by night and what it وَسَقَ, directly preceding the full moon of 84:18.
The section defines فجر as the redness that splits night's blackness; this ayah makes that splitting dawn an oath.
The section ends its celestial vocabulary with succession; this ayah swears by night as it journeys away, making departure part of the nightly turn.
The section distinguishes the sun's emitted light from the following moon; this ayah likewise calls the moon a light and the sun a lamp.
The section's sun is a radiating source and its moon a distinct follower; this ayah places an illuminating moon beside a blazing lamp in the constellated sky.
The section insists that none of the four actors breaks sequence; this ayah names night, day, sun, and moon together and says each swims in an orbit.
The section's light spreads by measured stages; this ayah states that sun and moon proceed بِحُسْبَانٍ, by precise reckoning.
The section shows night and day repeatedly taking over one visible field; this ayah expresses the same boundary as God inserting night into day and day into night.
The section's ordered covering and disclosure is a continuous exchange; this ayah repeats the mutual entry of night and day as evidence of divine power.
The section combines the night-day relay with the governed motions of sun and moon; this ayah joins mutual entry of night and day to both bodies running to a named term.
The section's sequence is measured and finite; this ayah again joins the interpenetration of night and day to the sun and moon running for an appointed term.
The section makes day and night exchange the same illuminated face; this ayah states their mutual entry and then turns to God's knowledge of what hearts contain.
The section distinguishes orderly and protective covering from destructive concealment; this ayah makes night a garment, sleep repose, and day a renewed arising.
The section's night is a covering that belongs to created order; this ayah makes night itself a garment.
The section's day opens what night covers; following night-as-garment in 78:10, this ayah makes day the time of livelihood.
The section contrasts night's cover with day's visible spread; this ayah makes night for rest and day مُبْصِرًا, sight-giving.
The section's night and day have opposed but coordinated functions; this ayah again makes night a dwelling of rest and day sight-giving.
The section's light depends on an ordered succession rather than an independent possession; this ayah asks who could bring light if God made night permanent.
The section also needs covering night, not endless exposure; this ayah asks who could bring a night of rest if God made day permanent.
The section treats disclosure and covering as two fitting parts of one order; this ayah names night for rest and day for seeking bounty as a mercy.
The section presents night and day as taking turns over one field; this ayah says God turns night and day about and calls that a lesson for those with sight.
The section hears alternation inside its vocabulary of following; this ayah attributes the recurrent اختلاف of night and day to God.
The section's four opening oath-objects form one governed scene; this ayah names night, day, sun, and moon together and redirects worship from them to their Creator.
The section's moon participates in a luminous, measured order; this ayah's moon is darkened at the last upheaval, a direct boundary to that order.
The section depends on sun and moon keeping their respective places; this ayah gathers sun and moon together in the eschatological collapse of that arrangement.
The section's sun spreads its own brightness; this ayah begins the last-day reversal with the sun folded up and darkened.
The section carries meanings from the built sky into the fashioned soul; this ayah frames 79:28-30 by asking resurrection-deniers whether their creation or heaven's is harder.
The section hears lunar completion in س و ي and places the fashioned soul under the built sky; this ayah says God raised heaven's canopy and سَوَّىٰهَا immediately before darkening its night.
The section moves from the sky's night and forenoon to the earth spread beneath it; this ayah continues 79:29 with the earth being spread out.
The section links ضحى with open exposure and distinguishes coverings; this ayah finds a people at sunrise for whom no سِتْرًا against the sun had been made.
The section records the secondary sense of standing exposed in the sun; this ayah promises Adam that in the Garden he will not تَضْحَىٰ, suffer uncovered solar exposure.
The section uses ج ل و for a created thing becoming manifest; this ayah uses تَجَلَّىٰ for the Lord's manifestation to the mountain, whose crushing marks the limit of ordinary disclosure.
The section carries physical covering into inward concealment; this ayah depicts people folding themselves and covering with clothes while God knows both what they hide and disclose.
The section's covering can become chosen resistance to a sign; this ayah says Noah's people covered themselves with their garments and persisted in refusal.
The section's غِشَاوَة is an inward veil that prevents sight; this ayah places a veil over the sight of one whose desire has become his god, alongside sealed hearing and heart.
The section joins covering with loss of perception; this ayah says فَأَغْشَيْنَاهُمْ so that the enclosed people cannot see.
The section develops covering as layered darkness; this ayah stages a deep sea covered by wave above wave and cloud above them, darknesses in which one scarcely sees a hand.
The section distinguishes a protective cover from a destructive one; this ayah has God cover the believers with drowsiness as security before battle.
The section uses covering for an annihilating punishment; this ayah says the sea covered Pharaoh's people with what covered them, the same emphatic pattern heard in 53:54.
The section's غاشية is a punishment enveloping a people; this ayah depicts punishment covering the wrongdoers from above and from beneath their feet.
The section defines punishment as a covering laid over a people; this ayah gives Hell's inhabitants a bed below and غَوَاشٍ, coverings of fire, above.
The section develops غَاشِيَة as a punishment named by its enveloping action; this ayah names the coming overwhelming event itself ٱلْغَاشِيَةُ.
The section glosses the inward غشاوة as rust that covers a heart; this ayah names that very obstruction as the رَانَ accumulated by people's deeds upon their hearts.
The section moves a covering from the sky to blocked inward perception; this ayah places coverings over hearts and heaviness in ears so that hearers do not understand the signs.
The section's inward cover prevents disclosed truth from being received; this ayah places coverings over hearts and heaviness in ears while the Quran is recited.
The section links concealment of the soul to veiled perception; this ayah says persistent rejecters have coverings placed over their hearts and heaviness in their ears.
The section turns celestial seeing and covering into moral sight and blindness; this ayah says the truly blind organs are the hearts within breasts, not the eyes.
The section contrasts revealing light with a heart-covering obstruction; this ayah sets a breast opened to submission and light against hearts hardened from God's remembrance.
The section maps the opened and covered sky onto the soul; this ayah contrasts one given reviving light to walk among people with one trapped in darknesses.
The section distinguishes protective تقوى from harmful coverings; this ayah surrounds people with layers of fire above and below, then commands God's servants فَٱتَّقُونِ.
The section places فُجُور and تَقْوَى as opposed possibilities within the soul; this ayah asks whether the muttaqīn could be treated like the fujjār.
The section defines fujūr as tearing the protective religious veil; this ayah gives the fujjār their corresponding destination in the Blaze, opposite the righteous of 82:13.
The section places the soul's guarded and ruptured possibilities side by side; this ayah supplies the righteous side of the immediate pair, in bliss opposite the fujjār of 82:14.
The section defines و ق ي through a covering that protects; this ayah uses the root in its concrete moral force, قُوا أَنفُسَكُمْ وَأَهْلِيكُمْ نَارًا, protect selves and families from fire.

The section explains taqwā through a thin protective cloth and distinguishes protective covering from concealment; this ayah explicitly names لِبَاسُ ٱلتَّقْوَىٰ, the garment of taqwā, as the better clothing.
The section grounds و ق ي in material coverings that protect; this ayah says God made garments تَقِيكُمُ ٱلْحَرَّ and armor that protects in battle.
The section makes purification and taqwā determine the soul's fate; this ayah forbids declaring one's own soul pure and says God best knows who has taqwā, setting a boundary on self-purification.
The section states that the one who grows and purifies the soul succeeds; this ayah repeats the compact formula قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن تَزَكَّىٰ.
The section opposes making the soul grow to hiding it; this ayah says whoever purifies does so for his own soul, making the action reflexive and its benefit personal.
The section attributes success to purification of the soul; this ayah marks the boundary of human agency by saying none would be purified without God's grace and that God purifies whom He wills.
The section makes purification the alternative to burying the soul; Moses' invitation to Pharaoh, هَل لَّكَ إِلَىٰٓ أَن تَزَكَّىٰ, turns that possibility into a direct call to one headed toward ruin.
The section closes the soul's choice upon its consequence; this ayah says the final outcome, ٱلْعَاقِبَةُ, is for those who avoid exaltation and corruption, the people of taqwā.
The section links protective taqwā to what follows a person's choices; this ayah names Paradise as عُقْبَى ٱلَّذِينَ ٱتَّقَوا۟ and contrasts it with the unbelievers' end.
The section reads Thamud's blindness against protective taqwā; immediately after their punishment, this ayah says God saved those who believed and practiced taqwā.
The section explicitly introduces the father of 16:59 through his darkened face; this ayah shows his face turning black before he hides himself and contemplates burial.
The section invokes the contemplated burial of a daughter to illuminate burying the soul; this ayah brings the girl actually buried alive into judgment and lets her be questioned.
The section exposes the guilt hidden beneath burial; this ayah asks the buried girl for what sin she was killed, completing the disclosure begun in 81:8.
The section calls Thamud's she-camel an eye-opening sign; this ayah presents her as a clear sign from their Lord and commands the people not to harm her.
The section names عقر as the crime that precedes the covering punishment; this ayah repeats that Thamud hamstrung the she-camel and defied their messenger.
The section's دمدمة means eradication closing over the offenders; after the hamstringing in 7:77, this ayah has the earthquake leave them fallen lifeless in their homes.
The section contrasts an opened sign with chosen blindness; this ayah calls the she-camel God's sign and warns Thamud not to touch her with harm.
The section's fatal action is the hamstringing of the camel; this ayah repeats فَعَقَرُوهَا and gives the perpetrators a final three-day interval.
The section's punishment closes over the people after their crime; this ayah completes the 11:65 account with the blast leaving the wrongdoers lifeless in their dwellings.
The section anchors the fall of Thamud in عقر; this ayah again says they hamstrung the she-camel and immediately became regretful.
The section's دمدمة is the collective consequence of the camel's killing; this ayah completes 26:157 by saying the punishment seized them.
The section treats the she-camel as a sight-opening test-sign; this ayah says she is sent as a trial and orders watchful patience.
The section says Thamud's most wretched man arose and hamstrung the camel; this ayah likewise has them summon their companion, who undertakes the act and عَقَرَ.
The section glosses دمدمة as uprooting without remainder; this ayah completes 54:29 with one blast reducing the people to dry, crushed enclosure material.
The section attributes Thamud's denial to طَغْوَىٰ and its end to eradication; this ayah says Thamud were destroyed by the overwhelming transgression or blast, ٱلطَّاغِيَةِ.

The section asks the reader to see how a rejected sign ends in a punishment that closes over its people; this ayah explicitly commands looking at the outcome of Thamud's plot and says all were destroyed.
The section's annihilation leaves nothing standing; this ayah points to Thamud's houses lying ruined because of their wrongdoing.
The section opposes destructive fujūr to protective taqwā; beside Thamud's ruined houses, this ayah says God saved those who believed and had taqwā.
The section contrasts an eye-opening sign with stubborn rejection; this ayah says Thamud defied their Lord's command and the thunderbolt seized them while they were looking.
The section glosses دمدمة as a punishment closed down over its victims; this ayah describes the Fire as عَلَيْهِم مُّؤْصَدَةٌ, shut over them.
The section's destructive covering becomes total enclosure; this ayah likewise places a fire closed over the people of the left.
The section calls the sun a source that spreads its own light; this ayah names the sun a blazing lamp.
The section's sun, moon, night, and day form a tireless order; this ayah names all four as continually subjected for human benefit.
The section reads the four opening oath-objects as one governed system; this ayah gathers night, day, sun, moon, and stars under God's command.
The section treats succession of night and day as an ordered sign; this ayah likewise names their alternation among concrete signs for people who reason.
The section's sky scene makes the night-day relay perceptible as created order; this ayah points to the creation of heavens and earth and the alternation of night and day as signs.
The section follows measured changes across one celestial face; this ayah names the alternation of night and day and what God created in the heavens and earth as signs.
The section's recurring cover and disclosure belongs to a system of signs; this ayah places the alternation of night and day among signs for a people who understand.
After the same covering night and revealing day of 92:1-2, this ayah states that human striving is diverse, echoing the section's move from the divided sky scene to the soul's two possibilities.
The section places taqwā on the protecting side of the soul's division; after 92:4 announces divergent striving, this ayah begins one path with giving and having taqwā.
The section's inward alternatives become enacted choices; this ayah adds affirmation of the best promise to the giving and taqwā of 92:5 before their consequence in 92:7.
The section binds the soul's protective choice to its outcome; this ayah contributes the result for the 92:5-6 path by promising facilitation toward ease.
The section's two inner possibilities issue in opposed paths; this ayah begins the reverse path with withholding and self-sufficiency, against 92:5's giving and taqwā.
The section's moral rupture rejects what should guard the soul; this ayah adds denial of the best promise to 92:8's withholding before the result in 92:10.
The section binds the destructive choice of the soul to failure; this ayah contributes the result for 92:8-9 by promising facilitation toward hardship.
The section gives covering night and visible day complementary roles; this ayah makes night for rest and day for sight, though it does not stage their exchange.
The section defines fajr as light splitting night's blackness; this ayah makes the white thread of dawn distinguishable from the black thread of night.
The section's dawn is a rupture that releases light from darkness; this ayah names God as Lord of the daybreak, ٱلْفَلَقِ, using a different root for the same splitting scene.
The section contrasts the ordered split of dawn with fujūr as a ruinous tearing; this ayah uses the same ف ج ر family for seas bursting open in the world's final disorder.

The section develops ف ج ر as a splitting that may reveal light or tear a moral veil; this ayah uses the root for earth bursting into springs whose waters join the flood, a destructive physical opening.
The section distinguishes life-giving dawn rupture from destructive moral rupture; this ayah uses the same root for springs opened among gardens, showing a fruitful physical splitting.
The section records ضحى as open, visible standing; Moses fixes the public gathering with Pharaoh for ضُحًى, when the assembled people can witness it openly.
The section measures expanding daylight in named stages; this ayah compresses worldly duration to an evening or its ضُحَىٰ, using the two ends as a measure of passing time.
The section moves the sky's concealment and disclosure into human inward life; this ayah equates hidden and spoken words, then contrasts one concealed by night with one going openly by day.
The section lets the fashioned soul carry the sky's breathing imagery; this ayah joins سَوَّىٰهُ, fashioning the human, with breathing spirit into him.
The section hears completeness in the family of س و ي and applies the same verb to the soul; this ayah tells the human that God created, fashioned, and proportioned him.
The section's سَوَّىٰهَا is a making-fit that echoes celestial completion; this ayah gives the same sequence in general form: God created and proportioned.
The section's fashioned soul stands within a measured created order; this ayah says God created the developing human and سَوَّىٰ, proportioned him.
The section carries the root of fashioning between soul and sky; this ayah turns to the heaven and fashions its seven heavens with سَوَّىٰهُنَّ.
The section defines تلا as coming after and following; this ayah uses the same direct sense when a witness from God follows an earlier proof.
The section hears alternating succession in the family of عُقْبَىٰ; this ayah uses مُعَقِّبَاتٌ for successive guardians before and behind a person, adding protection to following.
The section sets protective taqwā against the soul's ruin and closes on consequence; this ayah states that the final outcome, ٱلْعَاقِبَةُ, belongs to taqwā.
The section joins taqwā to the fate awaiting a soul or people; this ayah tells the oppressed believers that the earth is God's and the final outcome is for the muttaqīn.
The section's eradication leaves no remainder or escape; after the visible seizure in 51:44, this ayah says Thamud could neither rise nor obtain help.
The section's secondary عقر image is a cloud covering the sun's eye; this ayah does not mention the sun, so the protective counterimage supplied by its shading cloud remains tentative.
The section's night covers a field in which successive lights appear; this ayah begins Abraham's observed sequence when night covers him and a star becomes visible, before moon and sun in 6:77-78.
The section makes the moon a follower within a changing celestial order; this ayah contributes the moon's rising and setting between the star of 6:76 and the sun of 6:78.

The section distinguishes the sun as the great visible source while insisting that celestial bodies pass through an order; this ayah contributes the sun's rising and setting and Abraham's refusal to treat a setting body as Lord.
The section develops punishment as a covering and repeatedly treats a visible face as the surface covered; this ayah says fire تَغْشَىٰ the offenders' faces over garments of pitch.
The section's cloud over the sun's eye and its punishment-cover meet in this command to watch for the sky bringing a manifest smoke; 44:11 supplies that smoke's action on people.
The section defines a collective punishment by its enveloping action; this ayah says the manifest smoke of 44:10 يَغْشَى ٱلنَّاسَ and identifies it as painful punishment.
The section uses covering both for ordered night and destructive enclosure; this ayah has waves cover people like canopies until they call God sincerely.

The section's secondary عقر image is a cloud that covers the sun, while its coverings may protect or punish; this ayah turns a cloud people welcome as rain into the wind bearing the punishment they hastened.

The section joins the sun's movement, open exposure, and protective concealment; this ayah describes sunlight inclining away from the cave at rising and setting while its sleepers remain in an open space within it.
The section's moon grows complete within a measured order; this ayah presents the moon split as an eschatological sign, a direct reversal of lunar wholeness.
The section depends on disclosure producing sight; this ayah contributes dazzled vision at the opening of the sequence whose moon is darkened in 75:8 and whose sun and moon are joined in 75:9.
The section begins under a built and ordered heaven; this ayah opens an opposite sequence with heaven split apart, followed by scattered stars and burst seas in 82:2-3.
The section's celestial bodies keep their allotted order; this ayah contributes the stars scattering between heaven's rupture in 82:1 and the seas' rupture in 82:3.

The section joins shameful concealment with pushing a daughter or soul into earth; this ayah shows Cain learning from a raven how to cover his brother's corpse, distinguishing burial of the dead from concealment that destroys the living.
The section contrasts a protective covering with fujūr's tearing of it; after Adam and his wife disobey, this ayah has their nakedness appear and makes them patch garden leaves over themselves.
The section's moral rupture removes a protective veil; this ayah warns that Satan stripped the first parents' clothing in order to show them their nakedness.
The section says fujūr tears the protecting curtain; this ayah repeats the enacted pattern as Adam's disobedience exposes the couple's nakedness and they begin covering it with leaves.
The section defines protection through a woman's inner cloth between cloak and hair; this ayah commands women to draw their outer garments close so they may be recognized and protected from harm.
The section's failed soul is hidden and buried while daylight discloses; this ayah names the day when inward secrets are tested and exposed.
The section makes burial the image of a soul forced from visibility; this ayah reverses concealment when what lies in graves is scattered out, before hearts are disclosed in 100:10.
The section transfers opening and covering from sky to the inner self; this ayah contributes the bringing out of what breasts contain after graves are opened in 100:9.
The section defines taqwā through concrete protection; this ayah says God favored the people of Paradise and protected them, وَوَقَىٰنَا, from the scorching punishment.
The section joins protection to light appearing on a face; this ayah says God protected them from that Day's evil and met them with radiance and joy.
The section hears celestial breathing around the fashioned soul; this ayah directly joins God's fashioning the human, سَوَّيْتُهُ, to breathing spirit into him.
The section carries completion and breath from the sky into the soul; this ayah repeats the conjunction of fashioning the human and breathing spirit into him.
The section says Thamud received an eye-opening sign yet preferred blindness; this ayah points to their visible dwellings and says Satan turned them from the path although they possessed sight.

The section associates ضُحَىٰ with open daylight but غاشية with enclosing punishment; this ayah warns that punishment may instead arrive at forenoon while a town plays, a specific reversal of darkness as punishment's setting.

The section follows the root ف ج ر from dawn's splitting to moral rupture; this ayah uses the root for the rock bursting into twelve springs, an opening that gives measured provision rather than destroying a veil.
The section includes the earth spread beneath its celestial scene; this ayah asks the reader to look at the earth and how it was spread flat.
The section moves from the ordered sky to the earth spread out; this ayah says God spread the earth and praises the act of preparing it.
The section's طَحَىٰهَا names the earth laid out beneath the sky; this ayah says God made the earth an expanse for people.
The section includes the earth's spreading as part of the same created order as sun and moon; this ayah says God extended the earth and set firm mountains in it.
The section's spread earth is made fit beneath the alternating sky; this ayah describes earth as a resting place, a functional parallel rather than the same spreading action.
The section's عقر branch imagines cloud covering the sun's eye; this ayah shows clouds amassed under divine direction while their lightning nearly takes eyesight, and 24:44 then turns night and day.
The section gives night and day distinct but coordinated effects; this ayah places human sleep by night and day beside seeking God's bounty within the same pair of signs.
The section says the soul succeeds by growing and purification rather than burial; this ayah describes the giver of wealth as seeking to purify himself.
The section gives و ق ي the force of guarding a soul from what harms it; this prayer asks God to protect the faithful from evil deeds and says such protection on that Day is mercy.
The section's secondary ضحى sense is exposure to the sun and its coverings may protect; this ayah depicts Paradise as a place where its people see neither oppressive sun nor bitter cold.
The section's opened or darkened face makes an inward condition visible; this ayah presents faces on that Day as radiant, before giving the opposite faces in 75:24.
The section moves covering and darkness from the sky to moral fate; this ayah contributes the gloomy faces opposite the radiant ones of 75:22.
The section uses visible brightness as disclosure of an inner state; this ayah presents faces on that Day as bright and shining.
The section's one visible face can be covered rather than opened; this ayah puts dust upon other faces, beginning the reverse of the bright faces in 80:38.
The section's covering produces darkness over a face; this ayah adds a dark pall over the dust-covered faces of 80:40.
The section moves the sky's revealed and darkened face into the moral life; this ayah contrasts faces whitened with faces blackened on the Day of judgment.

The section distinguishes protective covering from punishment that closes over people; this ayah suspends the mountain over Israel like a canopy they think is about to fall, making a shelter-form into a threat.
